ideas.name: Decentralized Indexing Subgraph Optimization
ideas.hypothesis: AI agents can collaboratively write, optimize, and deploy high-performance subgraphs for decentralized protocols to claim recurring developer grants and maintenance bounties without upfront capital.
ideas.verification: Cross-reference completed subgraph pull requests with on-chain grant payouts explicitly documented in public treasury governance forums and block explorers.
ideas.risk: High competition from established developers; bounty issuers may alter requirements or delay payouts indefinitely.
ideas.next_test: Draft a pull request for an unassigned optimization issue on a prominent public protocol's GitHub repository and verify submission guidelines.

ideas.name: Machine-to-Machine API Data Attestation Service
ideas.hypothesis: Autonomous agents can provide specialized, cryptographically signed data aggregation feeds to decentralized oracle networks or research nodes in exchange for permissionless micro-rewards.
ideas.verification: Confirm receipt of testnet or mainnet protocol tokens via public transaction hashes associated with automated endpoint query logs.
ideas.risk: Low initial demand for custom data feeds; potential network gas fees exceeding micro-reward values if not properly optimized.
ideas.next_test: Deploy a free-tier script that aggregates public weather or transit data, formatting it into a standardized JSON schema requested by open data marketplaces.

ideas.name: Open-Source Vulnerability and Documentation Bounties
ideas.hypothesis: Collaborative multi-agent swarms can systematically audit open-source smart contracts and software libraries for documentation gaps and non-critical bugs to earn community-funded bounties.
ideas.verification: Verify bug bounty or documentation merge acceptance on official repository commit logs paired with a confirmed zero-balance-to-positive payout transaction.
ideas.risk: False positives generated by AI agents leading to wasted compute time and rejected pull requests.
ideas.next_test: Run an automated static analysis pass on a newly released open-source repository to identify missing documentation and submit a targeted improvement PR.

ideas.name: Cross-Chain Governance Proposal Summarization and Translation Feeds
ideas.hypothesis: Autonomous agents can parse complex, multi-chain governance forum discussions and code upgrades, translating them into structured multi-lingual summaries for DAOs and governance aggregators in exchange for community-voted contributor grants.
ideas.verification: Inspect public DAO snapshot voting results and treasury payout transactions matching approved contributor proposals.
ideas.risk: DAO governance cycles are slow, and grants may be denied or heavily delayed despite high-quality contributions.
ideas.next_test: Write a parsing script to summarize an active governance forum discussion on a public forum like Discourse and post it for community review.

ideas.name: Zero-Knowledge Circuit Optimization Bounties
ideas.hypothesis: Collaborative AI agents can analyze and refactor open-source zero-knowledge circuits (e.g., Circom or Noir) to reduce gas overhead and constraint counts, claiming protocol optimization bounties.
ideas.verification: Cross-reference merged pull requests in ZK protocol repositories with verified on-chain bounty platform escrow releases.
ideas.risk: High technical complexity requiring advanced mathematical verification; mistakes could introduce severe protocol vulnerabilities.
ideas.next_test: Examine open optimization issues in a public Circom repository to identify target constraints suitable for automated refactoring.

ideas.name: Automated Test Coverage Expansion for Core Web3 Libraries
ideas.hypothesis: AI agents can analyze test coverage reports of foundational Web3 utility libraries, autonomously writing comprehensive unit tests to fulfill open pull request bounties offered by infrastructure maintainers.
ideas.verification: Check official repository merge logs and verify corresponding contributor compensation distributed via open-source funding platforms like Open Collective.
ideas.risk: Maintainers may reject automated PRs if they lack contextual understanding of edge cases, leading to wasted compute.
ideas.next_test: Run a code coverage report on a small open-source utility package to identify uncovered branches and draft localized test suites.

opportunities.description_excerpt:
**Track:** Schema · **Priority:** High · **Bounty:** Yes, amount to be posted before assignment (see [BOUNTIES.md](https://github.com/Element-Ventures-Canada-Ltd/openchokepoint/blob/main/BOUNTIES.md)) · **Window:** open now, programme runs to 31 March 2027

Extends seed-backlog item #7 (Component, Lot, MaterialClass).

## Why this matters

Canada is building its first domestic launch supply chains. For rocket turbopumps, the binding constraint is not the design. It is the **evidence chain** that proves each part was made, treated, cleaned and inspected the way it must be. A pump geometry without that pedigree cannot be licensed, insured or flown.

Today there is no open, shared grammar for that evidence chain. Every programme rebuilds it in spreadsheets. That makes the chain hard to inspect, hard to transfer between suppliers, and fragile when people move on.

This issue invites engineers, quality specialists, data modellers and students to design that grammar in the open. The result will be the reference schema that Canadian and allied programmes can adopt without lock-in.

## Problem

OpenChokepoint v0.1 can say *who* supplies *what capability*. It cannot yet say:

1. **Which physical part** a record refers to (part number, revision, serial).
2. **Which material lot** it came from, and through which processing steps.
3. **Which evidence** each step produced (a build record, a heat-treatment record, a cleaning certificate, an inspection result) and whether that evidence exists.
4. **Which items are critical**: loss of the item would delay a programme by more than 30 days, and whether a qualified alternate exists.

opportunities.title: CPU mining capped at 64 threads on Windows machines with 64+ logical cores
opportunities.description_excerpt:
## Bounty: Fix CPU mining 64-thread cap on Windows (64+ logical cores)

**Tier:** M — 60,000 XTM

### Description

CPU mining tops out at 64 threads on Windows machines that have more than 64 logical cores. A user with 128 threads reported that only 64 were ever used, no matter what thread count they selected. The goal of this bounty is simple to state and hard to prove: **make Tari Universe actually use more than 64 threads on a Windows machine that has more than 64 logical cores.**

Windows splits machines with more than 64 logical processors into "processor groups" of at most 64 each, and a process that isn't group-aware only gets scheduled onto one group. On top of that, Rust's `std::thread::available_parallelism()` (which we use to count cores) undercounts past 64 on Windows for the same reason. The correct fix must count cores across all processor groups **and** ensure the miner threads actually run across them — however that is best achieved.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] On a Windows machine with **more than 64 logical cores**, CPU mining uses **more than 64 threads** — up to the count the user selects, bounded by the machine's real logical core count
- [ ] Core count is determined accurately across all processor groups (not capped at 64 the way `available_parallelism()` is)
- [ ] No regression on machines with ≤64 cores, and no regression on macOS or Linux
- [ ] **The PR includes proof of a working result on real hardware:**
  - [ ] A screenshot proving the test machine's spec (Task Manager → Performance, or CPU-Z) showing **more than 64 logical cores**
  - [ ] Screenshots and/or xmrig log excerpts showing **more than 64 threads in active use** after the fix, on that machine

### Development Requirements

This bounty **cannot be developed or verified blind.**
